profile.address: Rogers Run, Westover Hills, San Antonio, Bexar County, Texas, 78251
profile.reading:
This building at 10045 Rogers Run in the Westover Hills area of San Antonio, Bexar County, is a company-operated data center built for Lowe's Companies, the publicly traded home-improvement retailer headquartered in Mooresville, North Carolina. Lowe's first announced plans for a San Antonio facility in mid-2006, when it sought city council approval for a property-tax abatement tied to the project. Contemporary trade coverage gave differing figures as the deal evolved: an early report in June 2006 described a roughly $126 million investment requiring about 25 workers, while a follow-up in November 2006 described a $68 million, 100,000-square-foot building expected to employ about 30 permanent staff and generate as many as 300 construction jobs. The spread between those figures likely reflects the project scope firming up between the initial incentive request and the final construction package, though this page relies on the original announcements rather than an independently confirmed final cost. San Antonio positioned itself in that period as a competitor for large corporate data center projects, with Microsoft and PayPal reportedly evaluating sites in the same market around the same time. The facility was in fact built and remains active: current San Antonio business listings still associate the Rogers Run address with Lowe's, and Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation permit records show a January 2025 filing for a roughly $13 million renovation covering about 10,418 square feet, describing replacement of uninterruptible power supply equipment along with modifications to electrical, mechanical, architectural, and fire-protection systems in the affected rooms, with work scheduled to run through July 2026. That permit is a useful, if narrow, public data point: it confirms the facility is still an actively maintained, power-critical building nearly two decades after it opened, even though it says nothing about total current IT load or white-space capacity. As with data centers run by other large retailers, this facility exists to support Lowe's own retail, e-commerce, and supply-chain systems rather than to lease space to outside tenants, so no commercial specification sheet, capacity figure, or certification level is publicly published for it.

The long gap between the facility's 2006 announcement and its still-active status two decades later is itself informative: enterprise-owned data centers built to support a single company's internal operations tend to have much longer operating lives than commercially marketed colocation space, precisely because there is no external tenant base to attract or retain -- the building simply needs to keep working for its one occupant, which the 2025 UPS-replacement permit suggests Lowe's continues to invest in doing.

reading.body:
This facility at Rogers Run in San Antonio is a company-operated data center built by Lowe's to support its own retail, e-commerce, and supply-chain systems. The facility was announced in 2006 as a roughly 100,000-square-foot building with an estimated cost between $68 and $126 million, though these figures reflect the project's original scope rather than confirmed current capacity. A January 2025 permit filing for UPS replacement and electrical modifications confirms the building remains actively maintained and power-critical nearly two decades after opening, but no published IT load, total capacity, or certification level is available in the public record.

Because this facility serves only Lowe's internal operations rather than commercial tenants, it does not publish the megawatt figures, rack counts, or cooling specifications that would allow assessment of its current role in the AI scaling chain. The Texas energy context shows 18 facilities statewide with published power figures totaling 468 MW, but this campus does not contribute a number to that total. Without a published specification, it cannot be ranked among the state's mapped capacity or assessed for relevance to AI infrastructure deployment.

For a reader evaluating AI's dependence on grid and building capacity, this facility is not a data point. It exists, it remains operational, and it likely consumes significant power, but Lowe's has chosen not to disclose those details. The absence of published figures means it cannot be counted when measuring whether the grid constrains AI scaling in Texas or nationally.
